Compare the two opinions. In Kisor, Justice Kagan reasoned that “when 
a court defers to a regulatory reading, it acts consistently with section 706,” 
because “[t]hat provision does not specify the standard of review a court should 
use in ‘determining] the meaning’ of an ambiguous rule.” That was “especially 
so,” according to Justice Kagan, because Seminole Rock was “decided the year 
before” the APA’s passage and, thus, reflected “the practice of judicial review 
at the time of the APA’s enactment.” Justice Kagan also argued that Auer was 
consistent with the rulemaking requirements contained in Section 553. In 
Loper Bright, Chief Justice Roberts claimed that Chevron conflicted with the 
“independent judgment... required by the APA.”
If the APA requires “independent judgment” for judicial review of agency 
statutory interpretation, is there a reason to believe that it requires a different 
standard for judicial review of agency regulatory interpretation? There are 
three potential answers to this question. First, it might be that the nuances of 
Section 706 (or the background law of interpretation before the APA’s passage) 
allow for a different standard of review for statutes and regulations. Recall, for 
example, that the provision directs courts to “interpret constitutional and 
statutory provisions,” leaving out an express reference to regulations in that 
particular phrase. Second, it might be that, as Chief Justice Roberts argued in 
his Kisor concurrence, “the distance between the majority and Justice 
Cor such” is not large, such that both approaches are consistent with the APA. 
In a sense, the requirements imposed by the Kisor majority on Auer deference 
might have, by themselves, dispatched Auer deference as a practical matter. 
Third, it might be that Auer deference is, as Justice Gorsuch argued in his 
separate opinion, a “zombie precedent” that will be revisited in the wake of 
Loper Bright's reasoning.
3. 
The Constitutional Challenge to Auer. The constitutional challenge to 
Auer deference was similar, though not identical, to the constitutional 
challenge to Chevron addressed by some of the Justices in Loper Bright. In a 
separate opinion in Decker v. Northwest Environmental Defense Center, 568 
U.S. 597 (2013), Justice Scalia articulated the constitutional challenge to Auer 
in the following manner:
[Auer deference] violate[s] a fundamental principle of separation 
of powers—^that the power to write a law and the power to interpret 
it cannot rest in the same hands. “When the legislative and executive 
powers are united in the same person . . . there can be no liberty; 
because apprehensions may arise, lest, the same monarch or senate 
should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical 
manner.” Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws bk. XI, ch. 6, pp. 151-152 
(O. Pies ted., T. Nugent transl. 1949). . . .
